category: Product Management · AI · LLM · Consumer Technology
headline: Making local AI actually useful at home.
summary: Worked on an AI-powered NAS platform combining local models, intelligent file management, media discovery, privacy controls, and AI agents — during a 0→1 build that won the CES Asia Best Innovation Award.

metrics.label: Critical AI issues identified through evaluation

caseStudy.problem: Local AI systems had powerful capabilities but poor discoverability, unreliable tool calling, and unclear user value. The on-device agent could technically do a lot — but nobody could tell, and it kept timing out.
caseStudy.insight: Users did not want “AI features.” They wanted AI to remove friction from things they already cared about — media, files, photos, and privacy. The product had to disappear into an existing habit, not add a new one.
role: Interviewed 100+ NAS users to separate real product opportunities from feature requests.
Prioritized the roadmap for the AI NAS business unit inside a company-wide incubator, competing against ~100 other internal projects for investment.
Designed and validated the AI Home Theater experience end to end, from concept through a 3-iteration beta.
Owned model selection for the on-device agent and diagnosed a scaling defect in its tool-calling architecture.
Defined the privacy architecture that separated a fully offline volume from a connected service volume.

Built a working prototype of the Home Theater experience myself (FastAPI + SQLite + vanilla JS/CSS, zero build step) — continue-watching shelf, movie/series grouping, HTTP-range video streaming — to validate the UX before it became a funded roadmap item.

Reverse-engineered the protocol for an undocumented secondary display panel (USB-serial, no public spec) and built its driver end to end, turning it into a configurable dashboard — at roughly 80% lower cost than sourcing the OEM's own accessory.
constraints: Everything had to run acceptably on consumer NAS hardware, not a cloud GPU cluster.
Privacy was a stated product pillar, not a compliance checkbox — the architecture had to hold up under real scrutiny.
The agent's tool registry was growing faster than its ability to reason about which tool to call, and every added integration made timeouts more likely.

decisionProcess.heading: Finding the real opportunity
body: Rather than starting from “what can the AI do,” I ran structured interviews with 100+ existing NAS users to map where they actually lost time: finding a movie to watch, organizing a media library, recovering from duplicate or misnamed files.
Home Theater — AI-assisted media discovery and recommendation — surfaced as the clearest, most testable opportunity, so I scoped an MVP around it instead of a broader “AI assistant” pitch.

decisionProcess.heading: Diagnosing the timeout problem
body: Agent timeouts and runaway token use traced back to exhaustive API enumeration — the agent was reasoning over every available tool on every turn.
I proposed an MCP-based tool registry so the agent only reasoned over relevant tools per task, cutting tool-selection token overhead by roughly 80% and eliminating the timeouts outright.

decisionProcess.heading: Choosing the on-device model
body: Model choice had to balance quality, latency, and what would actually run on-device. I built a 6-dimension evaluation framework and A/B tested 7 candidate LLMs across 1,000+ prompts.
Qwen paired with Hermes scored highest (4.5/5) and became the on-device default; the same evaluation harness later caught 40+ release-critical defects before they reached users.

decisionProcess.heading: Prototyping before the roadmap slot
body: Rather than writing a spec and waiting for an engineering slot, I built Home Theater myself as a working prototype: a FastAPI backend with a single SQLite table for metadata, HTTP-range streaming so video could scrub and resume, and a shelf-based UI (Continue Watching, Recently Added, Movies, TV Series) in plain HTML/CSS/JS with no build step.

That let the 80-user beta touch a real, working product in days rather than after a full engineering cycle — the usage data from that prototype, not a mockup, is what won the case for full-scale investment.

solution: An AI Home Theater experience: on-device recommendations for similar titles, actors, and directors, plus IMDb-based subtitle matching, wrapped in a simple conversational entry point.
Auto Scan — ingestion-time indexing and tagging that cut manual organization and retrieval time by 90%.
An MCP-based tool registry that scoped the agent's available tools to the task at hand instead of the full catalog.
Continue-watching and movie/series grouping (with per-season episode lists), so the experience read as a home-theater app, not a file browser with a play button.
architecture: Dual-volume privacy design: an isolated private volume for fully offline data and models, and a separate connected-service volume for anything that touches the network — so users could opt into convenience without quietly losing the offline guarantee.
On-device inference (Qwen + Hermes) for recommendation and conversational features, with the MCP tool registry mediating access to file-system and media-metadata tools.
A reproducible evaluation harness (1,000+ prompts across 7 models) used both for model selection and as an ongoing regression suite.

The wider platform separated into an Agent layer (task planning, dynamic skill loading), a Model layer (a local, quantized multi-billion-parameter LLM with multimodal understanding), a Data layer (private RAG over the user's own files, vector search, full-disk encryption), and a Connection layer (NAT traversal so the NAS is reachable without a public IP) — Home Theater was the consumer-facing surface I built on top of that stack.

My own prototype ran on FastAPI with one evolving SQLite table — new columns added through idempotent migrations, never a breaking schema change — and HTTP Range requests for scrubbing and resume: deliberately boring, well-understood tech so the team could argue about the experience, not the plumbing.
productDecisions: Shipped Home Theater as a narrow, well-tested wedge rather than a broad “AI assistant,” so the team could validate real usage before expanding scope.
Treated the tool-calling defect as a product problem, not just an engineering bug — an agent that times out has no product value regardless of model quality.
Made privacy a structural property of the architecture (separate volumes) rather than a setting a user could misconfigure.
Chose to prototype in a throwaway stack (FastAPI/SQLite/vanilla JS) rather than wait for the production platform, so real usage could shape the roadmap instead of the other way around.

results.label: DAU penetration in beta, against a 5-interactions/week test bar
Feedback items synthesized into 3 product iterations
Best Innovation Award, contributed to by the privacy architecture

learnings: A model-quality problem and a product-adoption problem can look identical from the outside — the fix here was architectural (tool scoping), not a bigger model.
Validating one sharp use case with real usage data made the case for full-scale investment far more effectively than a broader feature list would have.
A rough, working prototype moves a roadmap conversation faster than the best-written spec — it turns “I think users will like this” into something a stakeholder can actually click through.

prototypeNote: Built end-to-end as a working prototype — FastAPI + SQLite + vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no build step — before it was a funded roadmap item.

secondaryFeature.title: An auxiliary-display driver for an undocumented USB panel
description: The NAS's secondary display — a small USB LCD bar — had no public protocol or SDK. I reverse-engineered its serial framing (a 5-byte header plus a raw JPEG, no container) and built a driver that turns it into a configurable dashboard.

Scenes — industrial telemetry, NAS status, a clock, weather, now-playing, a drag-to-arrange custom widget board, even a media loop or photo slideshow — are authored as ordinary HTML pages, screenshotted headlessly, rotated into the panel's native orientation, and streamed over serial. A new scene never needs a firmware change or a rebuild.
Reported result: roughly 80% lower cost than sourcing the OEM's own accessory driver, for a materially more flexible display.
pipeline: Pick a scene in the browser control panel
A small server renders that scene's HTML at 960×360 in headless Chromium
The frame is rotated 90° into the panel's native 360×960 portrait JPEG
Pushed over serial behind a 5-byte frame header — the undocumented part I reverse-engineered
The USB panel displays it, refreshed continuously

media.alt: Scene Library control panel showing 8 selectable dashboard scenes: industrial telemetry, NAS status, clock, weather, now playing, custom dashboard, media loop, photo slideshow
media.caption: The driver's scene library — each tile is a swappable dashboard for the panel.

category: Automation · Infrastructure · Internal Tools · Product Thinking
headline: Turning repetitive infrastructure work into software.
summary: Owned the roadmap for an internal GIS/CAD network design tool used by 200+ engineers, and turned repeated operational bottlenecks into automation adopted company-wide.

caseStudy.problem: 200+ engineers relied on an internal GIS/CAD tool for network design, but the workflow around it was manual: downstream signal recalculation, BOM assembly, and equipment-error checking all depended on someone doing the same repetitive steps correctly, every time.
caseStudy.insight: The bottleneck wasn't the design tool itself — it was everything engineers did by hand around it. Interviews with 30+ designers kept surfacing the same two time sinks: recalculating signal levels after a change, and manually pulling bills of materials.
role: Functioned as product owner for the internal GIS/CAD network design tool, translating feedback from 30+ users into a prioritized roadmap.
Identified manual downstream signal recalculation as a key bottleneck and defined a 3-click Python automation for tracing, recalculation, and verification.
Built an Auto BOM function that automatically recorded equipment changes as they happened.
Owned the prioritization model for a 30-person cross-functional unit, ranking requests by volume, urgency, and dependency.
Led a 20-person audit of 1,000+ optical nodes for DOCSIS 4.0 readiness.
constraints: Any automation had to slot into an existing, already-adopted GIS/CAD workflow — engineers wouldn't switch tools, so the tool had to come to them.
Errors in signal recalculation or BOM data have real field consequences, so automation had to be at least as accurate as careful manual work, not just faster.
Prioritization had to serve a 30-person cross-functional unit with genuinely competing, legitimate priorities.

decisionProcess.heading: Finding the bottleneck through interviews
body: Rather than assuming what to automate, I interviewed 30+ designers about where their time actually went. Manual downstream signal recalculation and BOM/equipment-error checking came up repeatedly, independent of region or seniority.

decisionProcess.heading: Designing a 3-click automation, not a new system
body: Because designers wouldn't adopt a separate tool, the automation was built as a lightweight layer that traced, recalculated, and verified signal levels in three clicks inside the existing workflow — cutting recalculation time significantly and manual errors by 25%.
The same logic pattern — trace, compute, verify — was reused for Auto BOM, which recorded equipment changes automatically instead of requiring a manual pull.

decisionProcess.heading: Scaling adoption
body: Both tools were rolled out incrementally across regional teams; the recalculation automation was adopted by 3+ regional teams, and Auto BOM went company-wide once report-generation time savings (about 50%) were demonstrated in the first region.

solution: A 3-click Python automation for downstream signal tracing, recalculation, and verification, embedded in the existing design workflow.
Auto BOM: automatic recording of equipment changes as designers made them, replacing manual bill-of-materials assembly.
A prioritization model for the 30-person cross-functional unit that ranked requests by volume, urgency, and dependency instead of first-come-first-served.
architecture: Python automation layered on top of the existing GIS/CAD tool's data model, so designers kept their existing workflow and tool of record.
Change-tracking hooks that captured equipment modifications at the point of design, rather than reconstructing them later from disparate records.
productDecisions: Prioritized automating the two highest-frequency manual tasks (signal recalculation, BOM pulling) identified directly from user interviews, over building new design features.
Chose incremental regional rollout over a single company-wide launch, using early results to build the case for wider adoption.

results.label: Reduction in high-priority delays via the prioritization model
Improved network-data accuracy from the DOCSIS 4.0 audit
Faster report generation with Auto BOM, company-wide

learnings: The highest-leverage product opportunities were hiding inside operational workflows nobody thought of as a “product” — they just looked like how the job was done.
Automation that respects an existing workflow spreads faster than automation that asks people to change how they work.

headline: Turning market noise into actionable signals.
summary: An experimental, AI-assisted market monitoring system built to identify abnormal trading activity, summarize signals, and help active traders understand market reactions faster.

metrics.label: Built through rapid prototyping and testing

caseStudy.problem: Markets generate far more data than any single person can watch. Active traders either miss meaningful anomalies in the noise, or burn out trying to monitor everything manually.
caseStudy.insight: The goal wasn't to predict the market — it was to reduce the cognitive load of scanning it. Traders didn't need another opinion; they needed the system to notice what deserved attention and explain why, in plain language.
role: Scoped and built the product as a personal experiment, from problem framing through a working prototype.
Designed the core loop: detect anomaly → summarize → explain → let the user decide.
Built a volume-anomaly detection layer, an AI explanation panel, and an alert timeline as the first testable slice.
constraints: The system had to stay explanatory, never prescriptive — surfacing signals without telling users what to do with them.
Signal quality mattered more than signal quantity: a feed full of low-value alerts would train users to ignore it.

decisionProcess.heading: Choosing what to detect first
body: Rather than building broad market coverage, I started with volume-acceleration anomalies — a signal that's cheap to compute, easy to validate, and immediately legible to an active trader.

decisionProcess.heading: Designing the explanation layer
body: An anomaly on its own is just a number. The AI explanation panel translates a detected anomaly into a short, plain-language summary of what changed and why it might matter, without predicting a direction.

solution: A signal feed surfacing detected anomalies in near real time.
Volume-anomaly detection as the first production signal, with room to add sentiment and order-flow signals.
An AI explanation panel that summarizes what the system noticed in plain language.
An alert timeline for reviewing what fired and when.
architecture: A lightweight monitoring layer that ingests market data, computes anomaly scores, and routes flagged events to a summarization step before they reach the feed.
productDecisions: Deliberately kept the product to a dashboard-style signal feed rather than stock-market clichés (tickers, candlesticks-as-hero), to keep the focus on interpretation over spectacle.
Treated this as a validation exercise for a product hypothesis — reduce cognitive load, not just add more data — rather than a trading tool to monetize immediately.

results.label: Detection and explanation components validated end-to-end
Self-funded exploration outside of full-time roles

learnings: Explaining a signal is a harder and more valuable product problem than detecting one.
Restraint — showing fewer, higher-confidence signals — is itself a product decision, not a limitation.

category: Plasma Physics · Electrical Engineering · Infrastructure · Software
headline: Engineering before product management.
summary: The industries changed — plasma physics research, electrical equipment engineering, telecommunications infrastructure, software automation, AI products. The underlying habit didn't: understand the system, find the bottleneck, build a better solution.

caseStudy.problem: Before product management, the work was hands-on: physics experiments, electrical hardware, and field infrastructure — each with its own constraints, materials, and failure modes.
caseStudy.insight: Every environment rewarded the same habit: understand how the system actually behaves, find where it breaks down or wastes effort, and build a concrete fix — a curve fit, a tolerance adjustment, an automation script.
role: NYU Tandon Plasma Physics Lab: designed Paschen Curve experiments isolating the effect of magnetic-field orientation on gas-discharge breakdown voltage, and built the lab itself from an empty facility to operational readiness.
Decom Electrical: co-engineered a 600mm-wide SF6 gas-insulated switchgear system, producing 3D models and assembly drawings in SOLIDWORKS and AutoCAD from concept through prototype.
A.T. Kearney: analyzed customer and store-performance data for a major retail client, contributing to a 15% sales increase.
constraints: Physical hardware has no “ship a patch later” — tolerance and assembly decisions had to be right before prototype build.
A brand-new lab meant building infrastructure (vacuum systems, safety integration) before any experiment could run at all.

decisionProcess.heading: From physics to hardware to infrastructure
body: Each role sharpened the same instinct in a different medium: MATLAB models for curve fitting in the lab; DFM/DFA and tolerance review for switchgear assembly; and later, workflow analysis for telecom infrastructure and AI systems.

solution: A working plasma physics lab, built from equipment acquisition through vacuum-system setup and safety integration.
A 600mm-wide SF6 gas-insulated switchgear system carried from concept to prototype assembly.
architecture: Not applicable in the software sense — the throughline is methodology: instrument the system, isolate the variable, fix the bottleneck.
productDecisions: Carried a bias toward hands-on validation — build the experiment, build the prototype, test it — into later product and engineering work.

results.label: Sales increase from Kearney's retail analysis
Fewer assembly errors from DFM/DFA review at Decom

learnings: Systems thinking transfers across mediums — plasma physics, electrical hardware, fiber networks, and AI agents are different systems with the same underlying discipline.
